name: Stripe style: one shard cannot elect a primary and takes down the whole payments API (2019-07-10)
description: The path of creating a PaymentIntent: merchant SDK (exponential backoff + jitter retries) → LB → four layers of rate limiting and load shedding (request rate per user, concurrent requests per user, a fleet reserve for critical requests, test-mode traffic dropped first when workers are busy) → payments API → idempotency record → DocDB proxy → sharded database (each shard a replica set) → circuit breaker → card network authorization. After a success the ledger is written and the webhook sent asynchronously. On 2019-07-10 a shard shared by the API and several applications could not elect a primary and stopped accepting writes; the API's compute was held up and most API requests failed. Sources: https://stripe.com/rcas/2019-07-10 , https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters , https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency , https://stripe.dev/blog/how-stripes-document-databases-supported-99.999-uptime-with-zero-downtime-data-migrations , https://stripe.dev/blog/ledger-stripe-system-for-tracking-and-validating-money-movement . The parameters are scaled down for teaching; Stripe has not published how it calls the card networks or where idempotency keys are stored.

notes.text: Try this: 1) Run the scenario: from second 20 the primary of shard 0 almost stops answering (300 times slower). With no timeout, requests waiting on that shard hold the slots of the API and the DocDB proxy, the concurrency limiter starts answering 429, and payments on the other shards fail too (seconds 20–47: about 85% fail). 2) Add a 300 ms timeout on api→docproxy only: worse (about 95%), because the proxy still waits on the database and its slots are not freed. 3) Also add a 250 ms timeout on docproxy→docdb: failures drop to about 18%, about the writes that land on shard 0 (70% writes × 1/4). This is what Stripe later called isolating the failure of a single shard. 4) Raise the merchant retries to 5 and watch retries multiply the load.

Simplified: in the real incident the shard could not elect a primary (writes unavailable). The simulator has no election, so "the primary is extremely slow" stands in for it. A bulkhead is one limit per connection, not per shard, so it cannot isolate one shard. There are no idempotency semantics either (resending the same key does not charge twice): here a retry really runs again.
